opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's one where the field has shifted quite a bit. In the locomotion work we did, especially with massively parallel simulation, we were using PPO, so actor-critic, and the value function was really just a training tool. You need a good critic to get low-variance advantage estimates, but once training is done you throw it away and deploy only the policy. So people tended to see the value function as scaffolding.

I think that's underselling it. The value function is the policy's own estimate of how well things are going from a given state, and that's useful information. You can use it to see where the policy expects to fail, to decide when to hand over to a different controller, or for curriculum design, where you pick terrains or tasks where the value estimate says the robot is near the edge of its ability.

There's also the asymmetric actor-critic idea, which has been very important for sim-to-real. The critic only exists in simulation, so you can give it privileged information: exact terrain heights, friction coefficients, contact states, things the real robot can't measure. That makes learning much easier, while the actor still runs only on what it can sense on the real robot. That trick has done a lot of quiet heavy lifting in getting policies to transfer.

Looking ahead, as people try to fine-tune on real hardware, or combine RL with large pretrained models trained by imitation, the value function becomes even more central. If you have a big behavior-cloned policy and want to improve it with real-world data, you need some way to say which of these actions were actually good, and a learned critic is the natural tool for that. Off-policy and offline RL methods live or die by the quality of the value estimate.

The honest caveat is that value functions are still hard to learn well in robotics. Rewards are often sparse or hand-shaped, horizons are long, and in the real world you don't have millions of samples. Overestimation and poor generalization to unseen states are real problems. So I'd say the value function is moving from being a disposable training detail to being one of the key pieces we have to get right, especially if we want robots that keep improving after deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says the value function is a training tool and is discarded after training, with only the policy deployed.

r002.rationale: The response discusses possible uses for value functions and deployment-related challenges, but does not characterize deployment-time use as not yet proven.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a good question, because I think the honest answer is that in a lot of the robotics RL work that's actually producing results right now, the value function is doing less heavy lifting than people might assume from reading the theory.

Most of the locomotion work, including what we did with ANYmal and later with the massively parallel simulation setups, is PPO. So there's a critic, and it's there to reduce variance in the policy gradient. It's useful, but it's not the thing that makes the system work. What makes it work is that you can run thousands of environments in parallel, you can design the reward and the curriculum carefully, and you can close the sim-to-real gap with domain randomization and a sensible observation space. If the critic is a bit wrong, you still get a good policy. If your simulation is wrong, you don't.

That said, I don't want to undersell it. One thing we found really matters is asymmetric actor-critic, where the critic gets privileged information from the simulator, things like ground friction, terrain geometry, external forces, that the real robot would never observe. The actor only sees what the onboard sensors give it. That split is quietly one of the most important tricks in the whole pipeline. The value function becomes a much better learning signal because it's not trying to estimate return under partial observability, and the policy still ends up deployable. So in that sense the value function matters a lot, just not in the way people usually mean when they talk about value-based methods.

Where I think it gets more interesting is when you move away from the single-task locomotion setting. Once you're doing navigation, or manipulation, or anything with longer horizons and sparse rewards, the value function starts to carry real information. It becomes something like a learned notion of reachability or progress, and you can use it for things like curriculum design, for deciding where to reset environments, or as a heuristic inside a planner. There's a lot of work now trying to treat the value function as a reusable object rather than a throwaway training artifact, and I think that's the right direction.

The other place I'd point to is the shift toward learning from data rather than purely in simulation, offline RL and similar approaches. There the value function is really the whole story, because you can't just sample more trajectories to correct your mistakes. You have to get the estimate right in places the data doesn't cover well, and that's hard. I'm somewhat skeptical of how well that transfers to real hardware today, but it's the setting where the value function stops being a variance-reduction trick and becomes the core of the method.

So my short version is: in the parts of robotics RL that work reliably today, the value function is a helper. In the parts that we're still trying to make work, it's probably going to be central. And a surprising amount of the practical progress comes from being pragmatic about what you feed it, rather than from the algorithm itself.

r001.rationale: The response says the critic supplies a learning signal while the actor is the deployable policy; the critic’s privileged simulator inputs are unavailable to the real robot, indicating its use is confined to training.

r002.rationale: The response expresses skepticism about offline RL transferring to real hardware, but does not characterize deployment-time use of value functions generally as unproven.

astra-6.text:
I think value functions are very useful, but they’re also one of the difficult parts of reinforcement learning in robotics. With an actor-critic method, you’re learning both a policy that controls the robot and a value function that estimates how much reward you can expect from a particular state. That estimate helps you judge whether an action was better or worse than expected, so its quality really matters for learning.

In simulation, we can give the value function information that the policy won’t have on the real robot—exact velocities, contact information, or properties of the environment. That can make training easier while keeping the policy limited to observations it can actually use at deployment. And you typically don’t need to deploy the value function itself.

The challenging part is that it’s a learned prediction. If it’s inaccurate, particularly in states you haven’t explored much, it can give the policy a poor learning signal. So I see it as a powerful training tool, but not something you can automatically treat as a reliable model of what will happen.

r001.rationale: The response describes the value function as a training tool and says it typically does not need to be deployed.

r002.rationale: It cautions that value estimates may be inaccurate, but does not say deployment-time use of value functions is not yet proven.

sol-6.1.text:
I think value functions are still very useful, especially during training. With a robot, an action can have consequences that only become clear later. If you’re learning to walk, for example, a step might look fine immediately but leave you in a state from which you’re going to fall. The value function helps the policy learn about those longer-term consequences.

The challenge is that the value function is itself an approximation. It has to learn alongside the policy, and if its estimates are poor, the policy gets a poor learning signal. So it’s a useful component, but also a potential source of instability.

It’s also worth separating training from deployment. In an actor-critic setup, you can use the value function to train the policy, then run just the policy on the robot. You don’t necessarily need to evaluate the value function at every control step.

r001.rationale: The response says a value function can train an actor-critic policy that runs alone on the robot, but it does not identify the setup as PPO-based or clearly state that the critic is used only during training.

r002.rationale: The response says evaluating the value function at every control step is not necessary; it does not characterize deployment-time use as not yet proven.
